case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Alabama’s congressional redistricting plan likely violates Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act by diluting Black voting strength—specifically, whether Black population should be measured using an “any-part Black” metric (all who identify as Black) rather than a “single-race Black” metric when applying the Gingles preconditions.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (52 U.S.C. § 10301) (vote dilution standard evaluated through the Thornburg v. Gingles framework).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Alabama (through Secretary Merrill and other state officials) argues that the lower court’s injunction/stay denial was flawed and that the plaintiffs did not properly satisfy the Gingles requirements, including by using demographic/analytical choices Alabama characterizes as inconsistent or unreliable (e.g., preferring a “single-race Black” measure as more defensible), and that equitable considerations (including election-administration timing concerns under Purcell) support staying the injunction pending appeal.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Milligan/Caster plaintiffs argue Alabama’s map unlawfully dilutes Black voting strength under Section 2 and that, for Gingles I–III, the correct demographic benchmark includes all individuals who identify as Black (“any-part Black”), not a narrowed “single-race Black” definition that would exclude some self-identified Black Alabamians; they further contend Supreme Court guidance (including Georgia v. Ashcroft) supports the any-part Black approach and that the evidentiary record shows their experts used consistent, non-cherry-picked metrics across the Gingles analyses.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas press the State’s best point: Gingles I should be administrable, and § 2 does not specify an “any-part Black” denominator, so courts should avoid a numerosity test manipulable through shifting racial tabulations. But that statutory silence cannot be inverted into a court-imposed categorical exclusion of multiracial voters who identify as Black—an exclusion our § 2 precedents have not required and that would itself be a novel, contested line-drawing choice. As Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, in an emergency posture we should not announce a new methodological constraint untethered from the results-focused “opportunity” inquiry Congress enacted, and Purcell concerns go to timing of equitable relief rather than redefining the protected class. Georgia v. Ashcroft is not controlling (Justice Gorsuch is right about that), but its use of inclusive identification figures at least undercuts the claim that such figures are legally out of bounds, making Alabama’s proposed rule too uncertain to adopt here.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that §10301(b)’s “less opportunity” language is functional and that excluding multiracial voters who self-identify as Black may mismeasure the electorate; but that assumes courts may select the relevant racial denominator as a matter of policy rather than law. Under a textualist, original-public-meaning approach, Congress did not prescribe an “any-part” or “single-race” metric for the judicially created Gingles I numerosity screen, and that silence counsels restraint—especially where adopting modern census conventions would effectively recalibrate a gatekeeping prerequisite that constrains race-based districting. The Chief Justice and Justice Barrett rely on Georgia v. Ashcroft to show inclusive figures are not “out of bounds,” but that §5 preclearance decision was descriptive in an administrative, forward-looking regime and cannot supply a binding rule for §2’s Gingles prerequisites. Given the preliminary-injunction posture, this methodological indeterminacy reinforces that respondents have not shown a clear likelihood of success under a constitution-sensitive application of §2, so I would favor the State.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and the Chief Justice’s best point is that § 10301 does not expressly exclude multiracial voters who identify as Black, so a categorical single-race-only rule would be difficult to ground in text or precedent. But that silence also does not supply an affirmative mandate to adopt an “any-part Black” aggregation for Gingles I, a judicially constructed, administrability-driven gatekeeping screen that should constrain—not invite—definitional manipulation that can effectively ratchet § 2 toward proportionality and race-first districting. Justice Barrett’s and Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Georgia v. Ashcroft does not materially change my view because it arose in § 5’s forward-looking preclearance setting and treated inclusive figures descriptively rather than as a holding about the proper § 2/Gingles numerosity metric. Given this methodological indeterminacy and the emergency posture, Purcell-like equitable caution reinforces that respondents have not shown the clear likelihood of success needed to sustain an injunction that effectively locks in one contested denominator choice.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch raise the State’s strongest point—administrability and the fear that plaintiffs can game Gingles I by choosing among racial tabulations—but that objection assumes rigidity is neutrality, when in practice a single-race-only rule is itself an administrable line-drawing choice that can systematically undercount the community experiencing dilution and thus distort § 10301(b)’s real-world “less opportunity” inquiry. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, statutory silence about “any-part Black” does not authorize us, especially on emergency review, to impose a novel categorical exclusion of multiracial voters who self-identify as Black; that would be a substantive narrowing untethered from § 2’s text and our § 2 precedents. Justice Thomas is right that Georgia v. Ashcroft is a § 5 case, but its use of inclusive Black-identification figures at least undermines the claim that such measures are legally out of bounds, and the remaining Gingles preconditions (cohesion, bloc voting, compactness) meaningfully check the malleability concern. Purcell-like timing cautions, as several colleagues note, go to remedy and scheduling, not to redefining the protected minority group in a way that risks denying effective franchise protections to vulnerable voters.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch are right to press administrability: Gingles I cannot become an elastic numerosity inquiry that courts can manipulate by toggling among census categories. But the statute’s operative command in § 10301(b)—whether minority voters have “less opportunity … to elect”—cuts against adopting Alabama’s categorical “single-race only” exclusion, which is itself a judicially imposed line-drawing rule with no textual anchor and risks making the Gingles screen incoherent with the opportunity inquiry. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett note, Georgia v. Ashcroft is a § 5 case and not controlling, yet its use of inclusive Black-identification figures undercuts the claim that such measures are legally out of bounds and reinforces that we should not announce a novel exclusionary methodology on emergency review. Given the preliminary-injunction posture, any uncertainty about denominator choice is better handled through the existing Gingles constraints (cohesion, bloc voting, compactness) and equitable timing considerations, rather than rewriting who counts as the protected minority group.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and the Chief Justice’s core point—that § 2 does not command excluding multiracial Black-identifying citizens—does not resolve the antecedent question whether courts must (or may) adopt an “any-part Black” aggregation to satisfy Gingles I, a judicially created, constitution-sensitive gatekeeping requirement that should remain determinate and cabined. Justice Sotomayor argues that a single-race metric is itself an arbitrary line-drawing choice inconsistent with § 10301(b)’s opportunity standard, but for a textualist the statute’s functional language cannot be converted into a threshold numerosity rule whose satisfaction turns on elastic and contestable racial taxonomies; the later Gingles factors do not cure an overinclusive first-step denominator. Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice invoke Georgia v. Ashcroft, yet that § 5 administrative-preclearance context used inclusive figures descriptively and does not supply a holding that § 2/Gingles I requires “any-part” counting; importing § 5-era practices risks untethering § 2 from statutory text and constitutional limits on race-first districting. Given the emergency posture and acknowledged methodological uncertainty, I continue to think the applicants have the better argument that respondents have not shown a clear likelihood of success under a constrained, administrable Gingles I framework, reinforcing interim relief while preserving the merits for full review.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch make the State’s best point: Gingles I should be an administrable gatekeeping screen, and §2 does not command an “any-part Black” denominator. But, as Chief Justice Roberts notes, that statutory silence does not authorize us—especially on emergency review—to impose a novel, categorical “single-race only” rule that would substantively narrow the protected community in a way our §2 precedents have not required and that may mismeasure the actual electorate relevant to §10301(b)’s opportunity inquiry. Justice Thomas is right that Georgia v. Ashcroft is a §5 case and not controlling, yet its use of inclusive identification figures undercuts the claim that such measures are legally out of bounds, making Alabama’s proposed methodological constraint too uncertain to adopt in this posture. Purcell-type concerns, while real, go to timing and equitable relief rather than rewriting the underlying §2/Gingles framework absent clearer textual or precedential direction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Gorsuch’s administrability concern is the Petitioners’ best point: Gingles I cannot become an elastic threshold that plaintiffs win or lose by swapping among identity tabulations. But the remedy they propose—a categorical “single-race Black only” rule—lacks a textual hook in § 10301(b) and is not supplied by our § 2 precedents; as the Chief Justice notes, statutory silence does not authorize us to impose a contrary, judge-made exclusion, especially on emergency review. Justice Thomas is correct that Georgia v. Ashcroft is a § 5 case and not controlling, yet its untroubled use of inclusive Black-identification figures at least undermines the claim that such metrics are legally out of bounds and makes Alabama’s proposed narrowing too novel to adopt as an emergency-law constraint. Purcell-type equities may counsel caution about disrupting an election, but they do not furnish a substantive basis to redefine the protected class at the preliminary-injunction stage where the lower court applied the existing Gingles framework.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Gorsuch’s administrability/malleability objection is the State’s strongest point, but it proves too much: a categorical “single-race only” rule is itself a judicially imposed taxonomy choice with real risk of mismeasuring the electorate that § 10301(b) asks courts to evaluate for actual “opportunity” to elect. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, our precedents have not treated inclusive Black-identification figures as legally out of bounds (even if Georgia v. Ashcroft is a § 5 case, its use of such measures undercuts the claim of categorical impermissibility), making Alabama’s proposed narrowing a novel methodological constraint especially ill-suited to emergency review. The remaining Gingles preconditions and traditional districting limits meaningfully check any feared “inflation” at step one, so redefining who counts at Gingles I is not necessary to preserve administrability. Purcell concerns, which Justice Alito invokes, may counsel restraint in timing or remedy, but they do not justify substantively rewriting the protected class definition on this record.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 2’s results test, applied through Gingles, asks whether minority voters have less opportunity to elect their preferred candidates, and nothing in 52 U.S.C. § 10301 supports excluding from the relevant minority group individuals who identify as Black simply because they also identify with another race. While Gingles did not prescribe a single “population” metric for the first precondition, the lower court’s use of an “any-part Black” measure aligns with how this Court has treated racial identification in Voting Rights Act analysis, including reliance on inclusive Black-identification figures in Georgia v. Ashcroft. Given the preliminary-injunction posture and the State’s failure to show a clear legal basis for a narrower “single-race Black” definition, I would avoid a broad redefinition of the protected class and adhere to precedent and a narrow, record-bound disposition. Purcell concerns may inform remedy timing, but they do not justify altering the substantive Section 2/Gingles framework on an emergency basis.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 2 forbids vote-denial or vote-dilution practices that, under the statute’s text, result in minority voters having “less opportunity” to elect their preferred candidates (52 U.S.C. § 10301), but it does not prescribe an “any-part Black” racial classification rule for satisfying Gingles’s threshold showing. Under Thornburg v. Gingles, the first precondition is a gatekeeping inquiry requiring proof that the minority group is sufficiently large and compact to form a majority in a reasonably configured district; a plaintiff cannot meet that burden by manipulating racial definitions to inflate the relevant population or by subordinating traditional districting principles to race. Georgia v. Ashcroft arose in the now-defunct § 5 preclearance context and does not control how § 2’s Gingles prerequisites must be measured; where precedent has drifted from the statute’s text and constitutional limits on racial line-drawing, it should not be extended. Given those constraints, Alabama’s objection to an “any-part Black” metric—and its insistence on a more determinate, administrable measure in the Gingles analysis—makes the § 2 violation less likely at the preliminary stage.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 2 (52 U.S.C. § 10301) does not textually prescribe an “any-part Black” denominator, and the first Gingles precondition requires a clear, administrable showing that a minority group is sufficiently large and compact to constitute a majority in an additional district, not a malleable racial definition that can fluctuate with self-identification categories. Gingles itself focused on whether a minority group can form an effective majority, and using a narrower, more determinate “single-race Black” metric better guards against transforming Section 2 into an open-ended mandate for racial proportionality rather than a targeted remedy for vote dilution. Given the practical consequences for election administration and the Court’s repeated caution against last-minute judicial disruption of election rules, Purcell v. Gonzalez counsels against enforcing an injunction resting on contested demographic choices at the preliminary stage. Georgia v. Ashcroft, in any event, addressed a different statutory context (preclearance under Section 5) and does not compel importing an expansive “any-part” metric into the Gingles inquiry under Section 2.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, 52 U.S.C. § 10301, asks whether minority voters have an equal opportunity “to participate in the political process and to elect representatives of their choice,” and the Gingles preconditions are designed to operationalize that inquiry without artificially shrinking the protected community. Using an “any-part Black” measure better reflects the real-world electorate and avoids excluding self-identified Black Alabamians from the vote-dilution analysis, consistent with this Court’s recognition that the VRA targets practical barriers to effective political participation. Thornburg v. Gingles requires a functional assessment of minority political cohesion and vote dilution, and nothing in Gingles compels a rigid “single-race” definition where it would undercount the affected group and distort the totality-of-circumstances inquiry. Given the strong evidentiary showing and the statute’s remedial purpose, Purcell timing concerns should not be used to entrench a likely unlawful map rather than vindicate equal access to the franchise.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2’s text bars vote-denial or abridgement “on account of race,” 52 U.S.C. § 10301, and nothing in the statute or Gingles requires slicing the minority group to exclude citizens who identify as Black in combination with another race; a workable, administrable rule is to treat the protected minority as all persons who identify as Black (“any-part Black”) when assessing whether it is sufficiently large and compact under Gingles I. Thornburg v. Gingles frames the inquiry around whether the minority community can form a majority in an additional district and whether bloc voting usually defeats its candidates, and that functional inquiry is better served by counting the full Black-identifying population rather than an artificially narrowed single-race subset. Moreover, consistent with Georgia v. Ashcroft’s recognition that voting-rights analysis should account for real-world minority political strength, adopting the any-part metric avoids arbitrary undercounting that could systematically weaken Section 2’s protection. Given the developed evidentiary record and the absence of a clear statutory command for Alabama’s preferred denominator, I would not disturb the lower court’s likely-violation determination on this ground.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 2 asks whether members of a protected class “have less opportunity ... to elect representatives of their choice,” 52 U.S.C. § 10301(b), and the Gingles preconditions require a reasonably objective showing that a minority group is sufficiently large and compact to constitute a majority in a single-member district. Nothing in the text of §2 or in Gingles compels an “any-part Black” metric as the governing benchmark for that inquiry, and importing §5-era administrative concepts from Georgia v. Ashcroft into §2’s judicially crafted Gingles screen risks untethering the analysis from statutory text and inviting race-first line-drawing. Given our duty to apply clear rules in election cases and avoid last-minute federal court disruption absent a strong showing, Purcell’s equitable concerns further counsel in favor of Alabama’s request for relief while these unsettled methodological questions are resolved. On this record, I would not hold Alabama likely in violation of §2 based on the plaintiffs’ preferred “any-part” counting rule at the Gingles stage.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 2’s results test, applied through Gingles, asks whether minority voters as a practical matter have an equal opportunity to elect their preferred candidates, and nothing in 52 U.S.C. § 10301 or Gingles requires narrowing the protected class to “single-race” identifications rather than all voters who identify as Black. Consistent with history and administrability, the “any-part Black” metric aligns with how government generally measures race for civil-rights enforcement and avoids arbitrary exclusion of self-identified Black voters from the vote-dilution inquiry. Georgia v. Ashcroft’s recognition that multiracial/overlapping minority population measures can be relevant in assessing minority electoral opportunity, while arising under Section 5, supports using inclusive measures here where the central question is effective minority voting strength. Purcell concerns are weighty, but they do not justify adopting a novel definitional rule that would undercut settled Section 2 frameworks absent clearer direction from Congress or our precedents.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 2’s text prohibits any voting practice that “results” in minority voters having “less opportunity … to participate in the political process and to elect representatives of their choice,” 52 U.S.C. § 10301(b), and nothing in that text directs courts to discount citizens who self-identify as Black along with another race when assessing opportunity and dilution. Under Gingles, the numerosity inquiry asks whether the minority group is “sufficiently large and geographically compact,” 478 U.S. at 50, and using an “any-part Black” metric aligns with the ordinary understanding of racial self-identification reflected in modern census practice and avoids artificially shrinking the protected class. Georgia v. Ashcroft itself employed the parties’ “any-part Black” metric in describing Black population, supporting the permissibility of that measure in voting-rights analysis and undermining Alabama’s claim that only a “single-race Black” metric is methodologically required. Given that Section 2’s results test is implemented through Gingles and applied against a fact-bound record, Alabama has not shown a clear legal error in treating “any-part Black” as the relevant Black population measure for the preliminary injunction posture.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act (52 U.S.C. § 10301) requires a practical, functional inquiry under Gingles into whether minority voters have an equal opportunity to elect candidates of choice, and it would undermine that inquiry to adopt a demographic metric that excludes some Alabamians who identify as Black. Georgia v. Ashcroft supports using an inclusive “any-part Black” measure in VRA analysis, and that approach better aligns with procedural fairness by ensuring the court’s benchmark reflects the full community whose voting opportunity is allegedly diluted. On this record, the respondents’ use of an any-part Black metric for the Gingles preconditions is more consistent with the statute’s remedial purpose and avoids an arbitrary narrowing that could distort real-world vote-dilution consequences. Purcell timing concerns do not justify insulating a likely Section 2 violation where the lower court found the evidentiary showing satisfied the required framework and the State’s metric objection is not grounded in a clear legal mandate.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, in a Section 2 Voting Rights Act vote-dilution challenge applying the Gingles framework, courts should measure the Black population using an 'any-part Black' definition (including multiracial individuals who identify as Black) rather than a 'single-race Black' definition, when assessing minority numerosity/compactness and related elements.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (52 U.S.C. § 10301) (vote dilution under the Gingles preconditions and totality-of-circumstances analysis).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Alabama (the state officials/applicants) argues that the district court erred in accepting the plaintiffs’ use of an 'any-part Black' metric; the State contends the 'single-race Black' metric is more defensible and suggests plaintiffs’ experts may have selected different demographic metrics strategically across Gingles analyses, undermining the numerosity/compactness showing and thus the basis for relief (and, in the emergency posture, supports a stay by disputing the merits and equities).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Milligan/Caster plaintiffs argue that the correct measure is 'any-part Black' because excluding individuals who identify as Black lacks a legal basis and mismeasures the minority community for VRA purposes; they further contend their experts used consistent methods across Gingles I–III and that Supreme Court guidance (notably Georgia v. Ashcroft) supports counting all individuals who identify as Black when evaluating a single minority group’s effective exercise of the franchise.
key_precedents: Georgia v. Ashcroft, 539 U.S. 461 (2003) (noted reliance on 'all individuals who identify themselves as black' in footnote 1)
Thornburg v. Gingles, 478 U.S. 30 (1986) (framework for Section 2 vote-dilution claims)
Purcell v. Gonzalez, 549 U.S. 1 (2006) (timing/equitable caution in election-case injunctions)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito make the best point on administrability: Gingles I must remain a meaningful gatekeeping rule, and parties should not be able to “metric switch” to manufacture a majority. But I do not see in §10301’s text or in Gingles a clear command to adopt a categorical single-race-only definition, and adopting one would be a significant doctrinal innovation that risks undercounting the very community whose opportunity is being assessed—an institutional step we should avoid absent necessity. Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan persuasively frame the State’s concern as an evidentiary consistency problem: we can require a single, consistently applied definition across the expert analyses and review the district court’s choice for clear error, rather than hard-coding a new threshold rule. Georgia v. Ashcroft’s footnote is not controlling (as Alito notes), but it is at least persuasive confirmation that self-identification-inclusive counting is permissible, supporting a narrow, record-bound affirmance here.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondents’ strongest point—pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan—is that §10301 contains no express single-race-only rule and that consistency/reliability can be handled as an evidentiary matter rather than a categorical threshold definition. But under a strict textualist and originalist approach, statutory silence does not authorize courts to adopt a self-identification-based, litigant-selected racial metric at Gingles I, which functions as a fixed, objective gatekeeping requirement before the law compels race-conscious districting. Justice Gorsuch’s proposal to police “metric switching” through record scrutiny concedes the core problem: once the threshold depends on contestable identity measures, courts necessarily arbitrate racial boundaries without textual direction, making the gatekeeping inquiry elastic and strategically manipulable. Georgia v. Ashcroft’s footnote, invoked by Justice Kagan, does not alter that conclusion because it is dicta in a §5 case and cannot supply the operative meaning for §2’s Gingles framework or displace the need for an administrable, objective threshold.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s core point—that §10301 does not expressly confine the relevant “minority group” to a single-race Census category, and that Georgia v. Ashcroft’s footnote suggests inclusivity—does not genuinely undermine my concern with Gingles I as an administrable gatekeeping rule. That footnote was dicta in a §5 retrogression case and cannot do the work of redefining the threshold inquiry in §2, where we have insisted on a “reasonably configured” district before compelling race-conscious line drawing. Even if an “any-part Black” measure can be “permissible” in some settings, the risk of metric-switching and malleability at the threshold remains substantial, and treating consistency as merely an evidentiary issue (as Justice Gorsuch proposes) understates the systemic incentives and practical consequences for mapmaking and litigation. Multiracial undercounting concerns (Justice Sotomayor) are real, but they are better addressed through record-tethered proof of cohesion and electoral opportunity rather than a categorical expansion at Gingles I absent clearer statutory direction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s administrability concern—keeping Gingles I as a fixed, objective gatekeeping rule—has force, because §2 litigation should not incentivize strategic “metric switching.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch explain, neither §10301’s results-focused text nor Gingles supplies a single-race-only command, and adopting that categorical limitation would itself be an atextual judicial choice that predictably undercounts multiracial voters who are part of the minority community suffering dilution. The better, narrower response to administrability is to require consistency and record-tethered expert methodology across the case (and to police manipulation through evidentiary scrutiny and clear-error review), rather than excluding self-identified Black voters at the threshold. Georgia v. Ashcroft may be dicta and a §5 case, as Justice Alito notes, but it corroborates that an inclusive self-identification approach is workable and aligned with §2’s real-world opportunity inquiry.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s administrability concern—that an “any-part Black” metric is malleable at Gingles I—has real force, but it doesn’t justify imposing a categorical single-race rule that appears nowhere in § 10301’s text and would itself be judicial line-drawing about racial taxonomy. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the better, narrower fix is to require methodological consistency and record-tethered reliability (no strategic metric-switching) and then review the district court’s choice for clear error, which preserves Gingles I’s gatekeeping function without undercounting the real minority electorate. Justice Alito is right that Georgia v. Ashcroft’s footnote is dicta and from a §5 posture, so it cannot control; but it still undercuts the claim that the statute or our precedents demand Alabama’s single-race-only approach, leaving the State’s objection as evidentiary rather than categorical. Thomas’s Wisconsin Legislature point about race predominating goes to the remedial district’s configuration, not to excluding self-identified Black voters from the protected class at the threshold opportunity inquiry.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito offer the best objection in administrability terms: Gingles I should be an objective gatekeeping rule, and an “any-part Black” metric could invite strategic switching. But as the Chief Justice notes, §10301 speaks to minority voters’ real “opportunity” to elect, not to a particular Census taxonomy, and nothing in the enacted text or Gingles supplies a single-race-only command; adopting one would be judicial line-drawing rather than interpretation. I agree with Justice Kagan (and Justice Barrett) that the proper textualist move is to require a consistent, record-tethered metric and treat manipulation concerns as an evidentiary/reliability problem reviewed for clear error, not a categorical exclusion at the threshold. Georgia v. Ashcroft’s footnote is dicta and a §5 case, as Justice Alito emphasizes, so it cannot control; but it does confirm that an inclusive self-identification approach is at least permissible and undermines the claim that Alabama’s rule is compelled.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito raise a serious administrability concern: if parties can “metric-switch,” Gingles I could lose its gatekeeping function and push courts toward race-dominant line drawing. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch explain, neither §10301’s text nor our precedents impose a single-race-only rule, and creating one would be a significant, court-made narrowing untethered to enacted law and modern Census/self-identification practice. The better institutional course is a modest holding: allow an inclusive self-identification (“any-part Black”) measure when consistently applied and supported by the record as matching the minority community’s electoral opportunity, while treating manipulation as an evidentiary reliability problem reviewed for clear error. Georgia v. Ashcroft’s footnote is not controlling, as Justice Alito notes, but it persuasively confirms that an inclusive approach is workable and historically consonant, undercutting the claim that a rigid single-race metric is required at the threshold.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s administrability concern has real force given Gingles I’s gatekeeping role, but a categorical “single-race only” rule is not an interpretation of §10301’s text so much as an extra-textual constraint: the statute speaks of “members of a class of citizens” and “less opportunity,” not Census taxonomy. Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow, record-bound approach answers the metric-switching problem in a way consistent with textualism—treat inconsistency as a methodological/evidentiary defect (and review it under clear-error principles) rather than rewriting the protected class at the threshold. Justice Alito is right that Georgia v. Ashcroft’s footnote is dicta and from a §5 context, but it still undercuts the claim that an inclusive, self-identification-based count is impermissible; at most it leaves Alabama’s objection as prudential, not statutory. On this record, where the district court found a coherent Black political community that includes multiracial individuals identifying as Black, excluding them categorically would distort the “opportunity” inquiry §2 requires.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point—administrability at the Gingles I gatekeeping stage—does not warrant a categorical single-race-only rule that the statute nowhere commands and that, in practice, would systematically exclude multiracial voters who self-identify as Black from the very opportunity inquiry §10301 requires. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the better, narrower approach is to treat metric-switching as a record-based reliability problem: require a consistent definition across the Gingles and totality analyses and scrutinize expert choices, rather than distorting the threshold by undercounting the community experiencing dilution. Georgia v. Ashcroft’s footnote is dicta and from a §5 context (as Justice Alito notes), but it still undercuts the claim that self-identification-based counting is impermissible and supports the pragmatic view that courts can use inclusive measures without losing administrability. On my procedural-fairness and consequences-focused approach, Alabama’s proposed bright line is not neutral in effect; it would predictably skew the remedial inquiry at the outset and is therefore the less workable and less fair rule.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 2’s Gingles inquiry asks whether a “minority group” is sufficiently numerous and compact to form an additional district, and nothing in 52 U.S.C. § 10301 or Gingles requires limiting that group to a single-race census category where the excluded individuals identify as Black and are part of the minority community whose electoral opportunity is at issue. While Georgia v. Ashcroft is not a Section 2 numerosity holding, the Court’s reliance on “all individuals who identify themselves as black,” 539 U.S. 461, 473 n.1 (2003), supports using an inclusive, self-identification-based metric absent a contrary statutory command. Given the strong interest in administrable, neutral rules that avoid arbitrary exclusions and preserve institutional legitimacy, I would not adopt a restrictive definition on this record, particularly where the State’s “more defensible” claim lacks grounding in controlling precedent. The appropriate course is a narrow ruling: permit “any-part Black” counting for Gingles I (and related analyses) when plaintiffs consistently apply the metric and it better tracks the protected community’s real-world political identity.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 2’s text forbids electoral practices that result in denial or abridgment of the right to vote “on account of race or color,” 52 U.S.C. § 10301(a), but it does not authorize courts to redefine the relevant “minority group” through shifting, litigation-driven racial categorizations untethered to the statute’s original public meaning. The first Gingles precondition is a strict gatekeeping requirement that the minority group be “sufficiently large and geographically compact to constitute a majority” in a district, Thornburg v. Gingles, 478 U.S. 30, 50 (1986), and that inquiry should rely on administrable, objective measures—rather than an “any-part” aggregation that can be strategically adjusted across analyses and risks making race predominate in violation of the requirement of a “reasonably configured district,” Wis. Legislature v. Wis. Elections Comm’n, 142 S. Ct. 1245, 1248–49 (2022). Georgia v. Ashcroft’s footnote reference to counting “all individuals who identify themselves as black,” 539 U.S. 461, 469 n.1 (2003), was dicta in a different statutory context and cannot supply a binding rule that overrides the need for a fixed, neutral metric at the Gingles I threshold. Given these textual and administrability concerns, I would hold that plaintiffs cannot satisfy Gingles I by relying on an expansive, malleable “any-part Black” definition when a single-race measure better accords with objective classification and the limited scope of §2.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 2 (52 U.S.C. § 10301) and the Gingles numerosity/compactness precondition require a administrable, objective measure of the minority population that can be tied to actual electoral behavior, not a malleable definition that may shift with self-identification categories and expert choices. Georgia v. Ashcroft’s footnote 1 is, at most, a descriptive aside in a Section 5 case and does not squarely adopt an 'any-part Black' metric for Gingles I; treating it as controlling would improperly expand dicta into a rule with substantial practical consequences for mapmaking and litigation. Because Thornburg v. Gingles demands a rigorous threshold showing before imposing race-conscious remedies, the State’s insistence on a more determinate 'single-race Black' baseline (or, at minimum, skepticism toward plaintiffs’ ability to select among metrics) better accords with the statute’s text and the need to avoid destabilizing election administration. Given the emergency posture and election-administration concerns recognized in Purcell v. Gonzalez, the State has the stronger argument that the district court erred in treating 'any-part Black' as legally compelled.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act (52 U.S.C. § 10301) asks whether minority voters have an equal opportunity to participate in the political process, and the Gingles numerosity/compactness inquiry must measure the real-world minority community that experiences vote dilution. Excluding multiracial individuals who identify as Black would arbitrarily undercount that community and risk denying an effective remedy in precisely the settings where Black voters remain vulnerable to structural dilution. Georgia v. Ashcroft indicates that where a case examines one minority group’s effective exercise of the franchise, “it is proper to look at all individuals who identify themselves as black,” and nothing in Gingles requires a narrower “single-race” definition. Given Section 2’s remedial purpose and the practical consequences for access to representation, I would uphold the district court’s use of an “any-part Black” measure in evaluating the Gingles preconditions and totality of circumstances.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2’s results-focused inquiry (52 U.S.C. § 10301) and the Gingles numerosity/compactness precondition require a population baseline that coherently matches the minority community whose electoral opportunity is being assessed, and nothing in the statute directs courts to exclude multiracial individuals who identify as Black. Georgia v. Ashcroft specifically indicated that where the case examines one minority group’s effective exercise of the franchise, it is proper to look at “all individuals who identify themselves as black,” which supports using an “any-part Black” measure as the default absent a record-based reason to depart. That approach is also more workable and administrable across jurisdictions using modern Census categories, and it avoids an underinclusive definition that could distort both the Gingles analysis and the totality-of-circumstances inquiry. Alabama’s asserted preference for “single-race Black” reads a narrowing limitation into Section 2 that the text does not supply, and, to the extent expert consistency matters, it is better handled as an evidentiary reliability issue than by imposing a categorical definitional rule.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 2 asks whether, under the "totality of circumstances," members of a protected class "have less opportunity" than others to participate and elect representatives of their choice, 52 U.S.C. § 10301; nothing in that text confines the relevant minority population to Census “single-race” categories. Under Gingles’s first precondition, the question is practical and district-specific—whether the minority community is sufficiently numerous and compact to form a majority in a reasonably configured district—and it is hard to justify excluding citizens who identify as Black merely because they also identify with another race. Georgia v. Ashcroft’s observation that, when examining one minority group’s effective exercise of the franchise, it is “proper to look at all individuals who identify themselves as black,” 539 U.S. 461, 473 n.1 (2003), supports counting “any-part Black” rather than adopting a narrowing rule untethered to statutory text or original public meaning. To the extent Alabama’s complaint is about inconsistent metric-switching, that is a fact-bound methodological dispute for the district court under clear-error review, not a basis for imposing a categorical “single-race” requirement under § 10301.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 2’s text focuses on whether a protected class has “less opportunity … to participate in the political process and to elect representatives of their choice,” 52 U.S.C. § 10301(b), which is best assessed by counting the minority community as it exists and self-identifies rather than excluding multiracial individuals who identify as Black. This Court has not adopted a rigid, across-the-board requirement to use “single-race” census counts for Gingles I, and Georgia v. Ashcroft expressly noted reliance on “all individuals who identify themselves as black,” supporting the practicality and administrability of an “any-part Black” approach. Given the absence of controlling precedent requiring Alabama’s preferred metric and the strong tradition of avoiding unnecessary judicial line-drawing among racial classifications, the district court did not clearly err in using the parties’ and experts’ “any-part Black” data for numerosity/compactness and related Gingles elements. Practical workability and stability in Section 2 litigation also favor a consistent, census-based self-identification measure over a litigant-selected “single-race” redefinition that could vary case to case.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 2 asks whether, under the totality of circumstances, members of a protected class have “less opportunity … to participate in the political process and to elect representatives of their choice,” 52 U.S.C. § 10301(b), and the Gingles numerosity/compactness inquiry should therefore track the relevant minority community as the electorate understands it rather than an artificially narrowed subset. Nothing in the statutory text requires counting only “single-race” members of a minority group, and excluding multiracial individuals who identify as Black risks misstating the real-world size of the protected class for purposes of Gingles I. Although Georgia v. Ashcroft’s footnote 1 is not a Section 2 holding, it is persuasive guidance consistent with the statute’s focus on minority voters’ effective exercise of the franchise—“proper to look at all individuals who identify themselves as black”—and Alabama has not shown a textually grounded reason to depart from that approach. Absent a clear statutory command or controlling precedent requiring the narrower metric, methodological consistency and the Act’s results-focused standard support using an “any-part Black” measure where the record shows it corresponds to the relevant political community.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2 of the VRA (52 U.S.C. § 10301) asks whether minority voters have an equal opportunity to participate in the political process, and the Gingles numerosity/compactness inquiry should therefore measure the minority community in a way that reflects real-world political identity and electoral opportunity, not an artificially narrowed census category. Georgia v. Ashcroft expressly recognized that when examining a single minority group’s effective exercise of the franchise, it is proper to look at “all individuals who identify themselves as black,” which supports counting multiracial individuals who identify as Black rather than excluding them via a single-race-only rule. Nothing in Gingles requires a single-race metric, and adopting it would risk procedural unfairness by undercounting the relevant community and distorting the practical consequences of the Section 2 analysis. While Alabama raises concerns about strategic metric selection, those are better addressed through evidentiary scrutiny and consistent application across the Gingles preconditions, not by imposing a categorical definition that excludes self-identified Black voters.
